title: Zips, buttons and closures that work every time

say: Zips, buttons and closures that work every time.
This is the video for module three of Fashion Finishing and Quality Control.
A closure is a moving part. It is opened and closed hundreds of times.

say: This module covers invisible zips for fitted dresses, regular zips where strength matters, and buttons and hooks that last.

say: An invisible zip looks like a normal seam, with only the pull tab showing. Buy it at least 2 to 3 cm longer than the opening. And do not sew the seam below yet. The zip goes in first.

panel.heading: Prepare before you sew
items: Buy it 2 to 3 cm longer than the opening
Leave the seam below unsewn
Finish the seam allowance edges
Fuse a 2 cm strip of light interfacing
Press the coil flat from the wrong side

say: Finish the allowance edges, then fuse a strip of light interfacing, about 2 cm wide, where the zip will go.

panel.heading: Prepare before you sew
items: Buy it 2 to 3 cm longer than the opening
Leave the seam below unsewn
Finish the seam allowance edges
Fuse a 2 cm strip of light interfacing
Press the coil flat from the wrong side

say: Open the zip and press the coil away from the tape from the wrong side, on a low synthetic setting with no steam. Do not let the iron touch the coil.

panel.heading: Prepare before you sew
items: Buy it 2 to 3 cm longer than the opening
Leave the seam below unsewn
Finish the seam allowance edges
Fuse a 2 cm strip of light interfacing
Press the coil flat from the wrong side
panel.rule: Press the coil with a low iron and no steam. Never touch the coil.

say: Place the open zip face down on the right side of the left piece, coil exactly on the seam line. Use an invisible zip foot, and sew from the top down until the foot touches the slider.

panel.heading: Sewing the invisible zip
items: First side: coil on the seam line
Sew top down until the foot meets slider
Close it and mark cross seams on tape
Second side: match marks, top down
Close the seam below, overlapping 1 cm

say: Close the zip and chalk the waist seam position on the second tape. For example, Tolu in Ilorin matched her waist seams within 1 mm this way. Sew the second side, also from top to bottom.

panel.heading: Sewing the invisible zip
items: First side: coil on the seam line
Sew top down until the foot meets slider
Close it and mark cross seams on tape
Second side: match marks, top down
Close the seam below, overlapping 1 cm
panel.rule: Sew both sides from top to bottom, so the zip cannot twist.

say: With a regular zip foot, start the seam below about 1 cm above the end of the zip stitching and about 2 mm to the left, so the lines overlap slightly without touching the coil.

panel.heading: Sewing the invisible zip
items: First side: coil on the seam line
Sew top down until the foot meets slider
Close it and mark cross seams on tape
Second side: match marks, top down
Close the seam below, overlapping 1 cm
panel.rule: Sew both sides from top to bottom, so the zip cannot twist.

say: A bubble at the bottom means the seam below started too far away from the zip stitching.

panel.heading: Three zip faults and their causes

cards.d: The seam below started too far away from the zip stitching.
The coil was not pressed flat, or the foot rode away from the coil.
The seam allowance was not stabilised with interfacing.

say: Visible zip tape means the coil was not pressed flat, or the foot rode away from it.

panel.heading: Three zip faults and their causes

cards.d: The seam below started too far away from the zip stitching.
The coil was not pressed flat, or the foot rode away from the coil.
The seam allowance was not stabilised with interfacing.

say: Waving means the allowance was not stabilised. Fix the cause before you resew.

say: Regular zips, with teeth on the front, are stronger and easier to repair. In a lapped setting, one fold hides the teeth and one row of topstitching shows.
Invisible zips look like an ordinary seam, best for fitted and occasion wear, but are less strong.

For example, Ruth in Kaduna is sewing a centred zip in a navy cotton skirt. She chooses 7 mm on each side of the seam, so both rows fall on the zip tape, clear of the teeth. A 7 mm strip of masking tape guides her.

panel.heading: Ruth's centred zip, safely
items: Topstitch 7 mm each side of the seam
Masking tape strip as a guide
Cross 1 cm below the zip stop
Stitch length 3 mm, matching thread

say: At the bottom she stitches across 1 cm below the zip stop, with a 3 mm stitch.
Never sew over metal teeth or the stopper. The needle can break and fly up. Walk the machine by hand near the stop, wear glasses if you have them, and keep your face back.

panel.heading: Ruth's centred zip, safely
items: Topstitch 7 mm each side of the seam
Masking tape strip as a guide
Cross 1 cm below the zip stop
Stitch length 3 mm, matching thread
panel.rule: Never sew over metal teeth or the zip stop.

say: For example, Joy in Calabar wants 7 buttons on a fitted blouse, the last one 42 cm below the first. Seven buttons make six spaces, so 42 divided by 6 is 7 cm apart.

panel.heading: Joy spaces seven blouse buttons
items: 7 buttons = 6 spaces
42 cm / 6 = 7 cm between buttons
Bust line at 21 cm: button 4
15 mm button + 3 mm thick = 18 mm hole
Pins across the ends before cutting

say: The bust line falls 21 cm down, exactly where button 4 lands, so the blouse will not gape.

panel.heading: Joy spaces seven blouse buttons
items: 7 buttons = 6 spaces
42 cm / 6 = 7 cm between buttons
Bust line at 21 cm: button 4
15 mm button + 3 mm thick = 18 mm hole
Pins across the ends before cutting

say: Her buttons are 15 mm across and 3 mm thick, so each buttonhole is 18 mm. Interface under the buttonholes and test one on scrap. To open it, put a pin across each end, and cut from the middle outwards.

panel.heading: Joy spaces seven blouse buttons
items: 7 buttons = 6 spaces
42 cm / 6 = 7 cm between buttons
Bust line at 21 cm: button 4
15 mm button + 3 mm thick = 18 mm hole
Pins across the ends before cutting
panel.rule: Buttonhole length = button diameter + thickness. Then test.

say: A flat button needs a thread shank, a little space for the buttonhole layer. Without it, the closure puckers and the threads wear through. Use double thread, and lay a matchstick on top of the button.

panel.heading: Sew every button with a shank
items: Double thread, small stitch to start
Matchstick on top of the button
Sew over it 5 or 6 times
Remove it, wrap thread 4 or 5 times
Finish with small stitches at the back

say: Sew over the stick 5 or 6 times. Remove it, pull the button up, and wrap the thread under it 4 or 5 times. Finish with small stitches on the back.
For group orders, wash one sample first, and check the buttons are still tight.

panel.heading: Sew every button with a shank
items: Double thread, small stitch to start
Matchstick on top of the button
Sew over it 5 or 6 times
Remove it, wrap thread 4 or 5 times
Finish with small stitches at the back

say: To remember. Buy invisible zips 2 to 3 cm longer. Stabilise, press the coil, and sew both sides top down. Never sew over metal teeth. Size buttonholes from the button. And give every button a thread shank.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Invisible zip 2 to 3 cm longer
Stabilise, press the coil, sew top down
Never sew over metal teeth or stops
Hole = button diameter + thickness
Every sew-through button needs a shank
